reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Fitzpatrick's Dermatology in General Medicine
clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive form of epidermolysis bullosa caused by defects in components of the hemidesmosome anchoring complex, chiefly laminin-332 (LAMA3, LAMB3, LAMC2) and collagen XVII (COL17A1)
Blistering occurs within the lamina lucida of the basement membrane zone, giving a junctional level of cleavage
The severe generalised subtype presents in the neonate with widespread blistering and characteristic exuberant granulation tissue, often around the mouth, nose, and airway
Prominent perioral and perinasal granulation tissue is a helpful clinical clue to the junctional form
Dental enamel hypoplasia is a characteristic associated feature owing to the role of these proteins in enamel formation
Extracutaneous involvement of the respiratory, gastrointestinal, and genitourinary tracts contributes to significant morbidity
Diagnosis relies on immunofluorescence antigen mapping and electron microscopy to localise the split, with genetic confirmation; management is supportive with wound care and nutritional support
reference.pathophysiology: The dermo-epidermal junction is held together by hemidesmosomes and their associated anchoring filaments, which span the lamina lucida of the basement membrane and connect basal keratinocytes to the underlying lamina densa. Laminin-332 and collagen XVII (the bullous pemphigoid antigen 180) are key structural components of this adhesion complex. In junctional epidermolysis bullosa, biallelic mutations reduce or abolish these proteins, weakening adhesion so that the skin separates within the lamina lucida under minimal mechanical stress. The same proteins are important in mucosal epithelia and in tooth enamel formation, which explains the mucosal involvement and enamel defects. The most severe subtypes cause extensive skin and mucosal loss with a high risk of infection, fluid loss, and airway compromise in infancy.
additionalDifferentials: Neonatal infective blistering such as staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome and herpes
Incontinentia pigmenti and other neonatal blistering disorders
Autoimmune blistering disease in older patients
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy with immunofluorescence antigen mapping localising the split to the lamina lucida
Transmission electron microscopy showing hemidesmosomal abnormalities
Molecular genetic testing of LAMA3, LAMB3, LAMC2, and COL17A1
Nutritional and growth assessment with monitoring for anaemia and micronutrient deficiency
Airway, dental, and mucosal evaluation for extracutaneous involvement
Microbiological swabs when infection is suspected
redFlags: Airway involvement with stridor or respiratory compromise from laryngeal granulation tissue
Extensive skin loss with sepsis, fluid, and electrolyte disturbance in a neonate
Failure to thrive and severe anaemia from chronic wounds and poor intake
Rapid deterioration in the severe generalised subtype, which carries high infant mortality
reference.prognosis: Outlook varies markedly by subtype: the severe generalised form carries high mortality in infancy from sepsis, respiratory involvement, and failure to thrive, whereas milder junctional variants are compatible with survival into adulthood with chronic blistering and extracutaneous complications.
pitfalls: Failing to identify the severe generalised subtype early, delaying appropriate supportive and palliative planning
Overlooking airway involvement heralded by perioral and perinasal granulation tissue
Neglecting nutritional support, dental care, and anaemia management
Mistaking neonatal junctional disease for infection
Assuming a uniform prognosis rather than recognising the wide spectrum of severity
management: Provide meticulous atraumatic wound care with non-adherent dressings, blister lancing and protection of fragile skin from shearing
Prevent and treat wound and systemic infection with surveillance swabs, topical antiseptics and culture-directed antibiotics
Give aggressive nutritional support and correct anaemia and micronutrient deficiencies to sustain growth and healing
Monitor and protect the airway for laryngeal and tracheal granulation tissue and involvement
Provide specialist dental care for enamel hypoplasia and manage gastrointestinal and genitourinary complications
Deliver proactive analgesia and coordinate care through a multidisciplinary epidermolysis bullosa team
Offer autosomal recessive genetic counselling with carrier and prenatal testing, and involve palliative care in the severe generalised subtype
